Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

decide verb

also make up one’s mind, I’ve decided, determine, I made up my mind to, I’ve made up my mind, I have made up my mind

classical

Caes. BG 4.6 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 300, 148
Traupman 103: I made up my mind to leave, cōnstituī hinc abīre

cōnstituō, cōnstituere, cōnstituī, cōnstitūtum

verb, third conjugation

decide, resolve (to do)

With an infinitive, or ut and the subjunctive.

Other words

  • statuō, statuere, statuī, statūtum — decide, make up one’s mind; settle (a question)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Ps. 549: rūs ut īrem jam heri mēcum statueram; Cic. Off. 3.70: magnī esse jūdicis statuere … quid quemque cuique praestāre oportēret

    Of settling between alternatives, often with an indirect question; with mēcum, of making up one’s own mind.

  • dēcernō, dēcernere, dēcrēvī, dēcrētum — decide formally, resolve; of a body, decree

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Verg. A. 4.475: dēcrēvitque morī; Traupman 133, 300

  • certum est (mihi) — I have decided, I am resolved (to)

    phrase: with an infinitive, or on its own before a future · also used · classical · Plaut. Bacch. 382: certumst, jam dīcam patrī; Cic. Rosc. Am. 31 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 103: I made up my mind to leave; mihi certum est, I’ve made up my mind, certum est mihi hinc abīre

    (locūtiō plērumque cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; also Cic., Liv.)

    Lewis & Short: mostly ante-classical, most frequent in Plautus. In this use it means “I am resolved”, not “it is certain” (for that, see sure).

  • dēstinātum mihi est — I have made up my mind

    also used · classical · Traupman 155

    Lewis & Short has the participle dēstinātus, “determined, resolved”; the impersonal use is like certum est mihi.

Examples

  • certumst, jam dīcam patrī

    I’ve made up my mind: I’ll tell his father this minutePlaut. Bacch. 382

  • Certumn' est tibi? — Certum.

    Have you made up your mind? — I have.Plaut. Poen. 496–497

  • Utrumque diplōma pater nōn in pērā Theodōrī, quippe quam puer in silvā relinquere solēret, sed ipse sēcum ferre cōnstituit.

    Dad decided to carry both passports himself, not in Theo’s bag, since the boy was apt to leave it in the woods.Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam

  • Hominī cōnsilium tunc deest, cum multa invenit.

    A man is stuck for a decision when he finds too many options.Publ. H 27

See also decision, choose, consider.
